title: Burning a feather pattern
subtitle: A beginner pyrography design for flat or spoon surfaces
excerpt: A feather is one of the best first pyrography patterns. The quill is a single confident line; the barbs are short strokes fanning out from it. The exercise teaches line control and shading at the same time. Works on flat boards, spoon handles, and bookmark blanks.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from standard pyrography teaching progressions; feather as beginner exercise is common across UK pyrography instruction manuals (Lora Irish, Suzie Millions) and workshop teaching in the British craft tradition.

glossaryTerms.definition: The craft of decorating wood (or other organic material) by burning designs onto the surface with a heated metal tip. The word comes from the Greek for fire-writing.
The central shaft of a feather, running from base to tip. In pyrography, the quill is the first line burned and all barb strokes fan out from it.

content.text: The feather is the standard first exercise in
pyrography
because it teaches two skills at once: a confident straight line for the
quill
, and a consistent fan of short strokes for the barbs. Both repeat predictably, so a beginner can see improvement within the first ten minutes.
Before you start burning.
Hot tip: a pyrography burner tip reaches 200 to 400 degrees C. Never touch the tip or rest it face-down. Use the stand between every stroke.
Fumes: burning wood produces fine particles and mild fumes. Work near an open window or with a small fan behind you pushing the smoke away.
Treated wood: never burn painted, stained, varnished, or MDF surfaces. Bare, unfinished timber only.
Burns: if you touch the tip, run cold water over the burn for ten minutes. Do not use ice or butter. A burn that blisters or covers more than 5 cm goes to A&E.
Wood choice

Pale, close-grained timbers burn most clearly: sycamore, lime (basswood), birch, and pear. Avoid open-grained woods (ash, oak) for your first attempts; the burner tip catches in the soft grain channels and the lines spread. Pine works but the resin pockets flare and the result is uneven. Sand the surface to 240-grit before you draw the design; scratches burn darker and show in the finished piece.
Drawing the feather

Sketch the feather lightly in pencil. The quill runs from base to tip, slightly curved: 8 to 12 cm for a bookmark or spoon handle. The barbs fan out from the quill at about 30 degrees, shorter near the tip, longer in the middle. A standard flight feather is widest at two-thirds of its length from the base. Erase any heavy pencil marks; the graphite can smear when burned.
Burning the quill

Set the burner to medium heat. Test on a scrap piece first: the tip should leave a mid-brown line in two or three seconds without scorching. Place the tip at the base of the quill line and draw it steadily toward the tip, keeping consistent pressure. A faster stroke burns lighter; a slower stroke burns darker. The quill should be the darkest line in the finished feather.
Burning the barbs

Work from the quill outward on each barb, not from the tip inward. Place the tip at the quill and draw it out in a single stroke, lifting cleanly at the barb tip. Barb strokes should fan slightly, with each barb nearly parallel to its neighbour. Keep the heat slightly lower than for the quill; barbs are lighter than the central shaft. Work all the barbs on one side first, then the other.
Shading

Once all the lines are burned, shade the underside of each barb with a slow, light circular stroke. This gives the feather a three-dimensional look. Shade only the lower half of each barb; the upper half stays pale. A final pass along the quill at slightly higher heat darkens it relative to the barbs.

attrs.symptom: The lines are spreading and fuzzy rather than crisp
attrs.cause: Heat is too high or the tip is moving too fast.
attrs.fix: Reduce the heat setting by one notch. Test on a scrap piece: a crisp line at medium speed is the target. Clean the tip on fine sandpaper if carbon build-up is blunting it.

attrs.symptom: The barb strokes are uneven in length and angle
attrs.cause: Drawing the stroke at an inconsistent angle to the quill.
attrs.fix: Rule faint pencil guidelines at 30 degrees from the quill before burning. Erase after burning is complete.

attrs.symptom: Dark spots where barbs meet the quill
attrs.cause: The tip is pausing at the start of each stroke before moving.
attrs.fix: Begin moving the tip the moment it touches the wood. A still hot tip burns a spot; a moving tip burns a line.
